Item battery table

Source: R/table_battery.R
table_battery.Rd

Tabulates a battery of items answered on one common scale, such as a Likert grid or the "array" question of a survey tool: one row per item and one column per level of the scale, with the row percentages of each item, an optional column adding up some levels (top), and the base of each row (n). The items are selected with tidyselect syntax.

With by, each group gets a block of columns, and each item gets a test of independence of the item and the group (the chi-squared, or Fisher's exact test when an expected count is below 5), adjusted for the family of the items by Holm's method.

Multiple output formats are available via output: a printed ASCII table ("default"), a wide or long numeric data.frame ("data.frame", "long"), or publication-ready tables ("tinytable", "gt", "flextable", "excel", "clipboard", "word").

Usage

table_battery(
  data,
  select,
  by = NULL,
  levels = NULL,
  top = NULL,
  sort = "",
  drop_na = TRUE,
  show_n = TRUE,
  weights = NULL,
  test = c("auto", "chisq", "fisher", "midp", "n1"),
  p_value = NULL,
  p_adjust = "holm",
  labels = getOption("spicy.var_labels", FALSE),
  note_labels = NULL,
  percent_digits = 1,
  p_digits = 3,
  decimal_mark = ".",
  align = c("decimal", "center", "right"),
  title = NULL,
  note = NULL,
  note_add = NULL,
  output = c("default", "data.frame", "long", "tinytable", "gt", "flextable", "excel",
    "clipboard", "word"),
  excel_path = NULL,
  excel_sheet = NULL,
  clipboard_delim = "\t",
  word_path = NULL,
  style = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per respondent.

select

The items of the battery, one column per item, in tidyselect syntax or as a character vector of column names. Their order is the order of the rows, unless sort sorts them. The by and weights columns are not part of the selection: a selection helper skips them, and naming one, or giving its position, is an error. A name that is not a column of data is an error (class spicy_missing_column), and so is an empty selection. The items share one scale; see Items and levels.

by

Optional grouping column, unquoted or as a string. Factor levels keep their declared order; any other column is sorted, as in table_categorical(). Rows with a missing by are removed from the whole table, and the note gives their count ("Missing values removed: sex (2)."); a by that no observation holds is an error (class spicy_invalid_data).

levels

The scale: the levels to show, in the order of the columns. NULL (the default) reads the scale from the items (see Items and levels). Given, levels is the scale whatever the items hold: a level that no item holds shows at 0, and any other answer, observed or declared, is left out of the percentages and the base, and the note names it. levels is the way to keep a "Don't know" answer out of the base, and to give numeric or text items a level nobody chose (levels = 1:5). The entries are written as the table shows the answers: for a labelled column, the "[code] label" string. An entry that no item declares or holds may be a typo: it keeps its column, at 0, with a warning (class spicy_unknown_name). A level that a factor declares and nobody chose does not warn, nor does a number within the values the numeric items hold (3 on a 1-5 scale); a number outside them does.

top

The levels the summary column adds up, for example top = c("Strongly agree", "Agree"). The column follows the levels; its header is the list of the levels joined by " + ", in the order of top, and its value is the sum of their percentages. Each entry must be one of the levels shown (see levels); another value is an error. Without by, a top of one level would repeat the column of that level, and is an error. NULL (the default) adds no column.

sort

The order of the rows, in the suffix grammar of freq() and table_multiresponse(), + for increasing and - for decreasing order:

  • "" (the default): the order of select;

  • "+" / "-": by the summary column of top, or, without top, by the first level shown;

  • "top+" / "top-": by the summary column (needs top);

  • "name+" / "name-": by the label of the item, in the C locale, the same on every platform (capitals before lower case);

  • "<level>+" / "<level>-": by the percentage of a level shown, for example sort = "Strongly agree-".

With by, the percentages are those of all the groups together. Items with the same value keep the order of select, and an item without data sorts last. The keywords are read first: "name+" sorts on the labels even when a level is called "name", and "top+" on the summary column even when a level is called "top". A level or a keyword without its direction ("Agree", "top") has two readings, and is an error that gives both. Any other value is an error.

drop_na

Logical. If TRUE (the default), the missing answers to an item leave its base: its percentages are on its valid answers, and its n counts them. If FALSE, a last column of missing answers ("(Missing)") follows the levels, and the base of each item is every row, its missing answers included.

show_n

Logical. If TRUE (the default), each row (each group block under by) ends with n, the base of its percentages.

weights

Optional frequency weights, as in table_categorical(): NULL (the default), a numeric vector of length nrow(data), or a single column of data, unquoted or as a string. The counts, the percentages, n and the tests are weighted. Rows with an NA weight leave the table, and the note says how many. Fisher's exact test needs whole numbers: see Tests. For survey weights, the percentages are right but the tests are not, which need the design.

test

The test of each item's p-value, as in table_categorical(): "auto" (the default) takes Pearson's chi-squared test when every expected count of the item's table is at least 5 and Fisher's exact test otherwise; "chisq" and "fisher" take one test for every item; "midp" takes the Fisher mid-p test for an item whose table is 2x2; "n1" takes the N-1 chi-squared test for a 2x2 table whose expected counts are all at least 1, and Fisher's exact test otherwise. A table that is not 2x2 follows "auto" under "midp" and "n1". The note names the test of each item. Ignored, with a warning, when the table runs no test.

p_value

Logical or NULL. With by, NULL (the default) and TRUE show the p column of the item tests; FALSE removes it from every output, the test columns of the long output included. Ignored without by, with a warning when TRUE: the table runs no test without groups to compare.

p_adjust

Multiple-comparison adjustment of the p column, applied to the family of the items tested: "holm" (the default), "none", or another method of stats::p.adjust() ("hochberg", "hommel", "bonferroni", "BH" / "fdr", "BY"), as in table_multiresponse(). See Multiple-comparison adjustment. Typing it when the table has no test to adjust (no by, or p_value = FALSE) is an error.

labels

How each variable is named in the table: in the rows, in the title, and in the notes. Four forms:

  • labels = FALSE shows the column name.

  • labels = TRUE shows the column's label attribute (as set by haven, labelled, or label_from_names()) when it is present, not NA, and not empty, and the column name otherwise.

  • labels = c(bmi = "Body mass index"), a named character vector, gives the columns it names these labels. Every other column follows options(spicy.var_labels): its name when the option is unset or FALSE, its label attribute when it is TRUE.

  • labels = var_labels(bmi = "BMI (kg/m2)") gives the columns it names these labels, and every other column its label attribute, whatever the option says. var_labels() alone is labels = TRUE.

A name that matches no column of the table warns (class spicy_unknown_name) and is left out, so one vector can still serve every table of a project. The default reads options(spicy.var_labels), and a TRUE or FALSE typed in the call wins over it. Any other value, NULL included, is an error. A variable label documents the data file; a published table carries the wording you set here. note_labels gives a variable a shorter label in the title and the notes.

note_labels

The label a variable takes where the table names it in a sentence, in the title and in the notes, in place of the one labels gives it: a named character vector, note_labels = c(sex = "sex at birth"), or a var_labels() object, which reads as one. labels can then name a row with a whole question while the note says "Missing values removed: sex at birth (2).". The rows, the column headers and the spanners keep the labels of labels, and so do the title and the notes for a variable note_labels does not name. A name that matches no column warns and is left out, as in labels, and NULL (the default) renames nothing. A note label that another variable of the table shows is an error (class spicy_label_collision): choose another one, or relabel the other variable.

percent_digits

Number of digits for percentages in report outputs. Defaults to 1. A whole number: a fraction is an error, as for every *_digits argument.

p_digits

Integer >= 1. Number of decimal places used to render p-values in the p column (default: 3, the APA Publication Manual standard). Both the displayed precision and the small-p threshold derive from this argument: p_digits = 3 prints .045 and <.001; p_digits = 4 prints .0451 and <.0001. Leading zeros are always stripped, following APA convention.

decimal_mark

The decimal mark, a single character: "." (the default) or "," in most styles; the Lancet style of spicy_style() uses the middle dot.

align

Horizontal alignment of the numeric columns in the console and in the rendered outputs: "decimal" (the default), "center", or "right", as in table_categorical().

title

The table title. NULL (the default) gives "Item battery", followed by "by" and the by variable under the labels contract (or its label in note_labels); a single string replaces it, and FALSE removes it, as in table_multiresponse().

note

The table note. NULL (the default) builds it, opening with "Note.": the direction of the percentages, the base, the levels left out, the weights, the rows removed and the items without data, then the tests, and the sentences of note_add. A single string replaces it, printed as typed after the lead-in ("Note.", unless the string opens with one), note_add after it, and FALSE removes it, as in every table function.

note_add

Sentences to add to the note: a character vector of one or more strings, each printed as typed (no period is added) and joined to the note by a space. They close its paragraph, after the definitions of the abbreviations and before the legend of the stars, in every output and in attr(x, "note"), and the sentences the table writes stay. With a string in note, they follow it, so a wrapper can add a house sentence to every table while one table replaces its note. An NA or an empty string is an error, and so is note_add with note = FALSE, which leaves no note to add to.

output

Output format. One of:

  • "default" (an ASCII table object, printed when the call is bare)

  • "data.frame" (the displayed table, numeric)

  • "long" (a long numeric data.frame)

  • "tinytable" (requires tinytable)

  • "gt" (requires gt)

  • "flextable" (requires flextable)

  • "excel" (requires openxlsx2)

  • "clipboard" (requires clipr)

  • "word" (requires flextable and officer)

excel_path

Path for output = "excel", ending in ".xlsx", in a directory that exists. Defaults to NULL.

excel_sheet

Sheet name for Excel export. NULL (the default) uses "Item battery".

clipboard_delim

Delimiter for clipboard text export. Defaults to "\t". A cell holding the delimiter itself, a double quote or a line break is quoted RFC 4180-style, so the grid survives whatever delimiter you choose.

word_path

File path for output = "word". Defaults to NULL.

style

A journal style: a theme name ("jama", "nejm", "lancet", "annals", "apa", "aer"), a spicy_style() object, or NULL (the default). A style only changes DEFAULTS – any argument you pass explicitly wins over it. Set options(spicy.style = ) for document-wide scope. A theme covers numeric formatting, the word that opens the note and the abbreviations the note defines, not full editorial conformity; ?spicy_style lists the exact rules each one encodes and the official document they come from. An unknown name is an error.

Value

Depends on output:

  • "default": a spicy_battery_table (a data.frame subclass), with the rendering metadata as attributes, returned visibly, so a bare call prints the ASCII table.

  • "data.frame": the displayed table with its numbers, what as.data.frame() of the default object returns: one row per item, with columns variable (the item's column), label (the label the row displays), then the printed columns: one percentage per level shown, (Missing) under drop_na = FALSE, the summary column of top (named by its header, "Strongly agree + Agree") and n, each prefixed with the group under by ("Female Agree", "Female n"), and p with p_value.

  • "long": one row per item, group and level, with columns variable, label, group (with by), level (the level, or the label of the column of missing answers), .row_role ("level", or "missing" for the missing answers), n (the count, weighted under weights) and pct (its percentage of the base), and, when the tests ran, test_type ("chi_squared", "n1_chi_squared", "fisher_exact", "fisher_midp", "fisher_exact_mc"), statistic and df (NA for an exact test), p.value, and p_unadjusted under an adjustment. The summary column is not part of it: it is the sum of the levels of top.

  • "tinytable", "gt", "flextable": the rendered table object.

  • "excel" / "word": writes to disk and returns the file path invisibly.

  • "clipboard": copies the table and returns the display data.frame invisibly.

The default object and the data frames carry the note as printed in attr(x, "note") (its lead-in included, NULL under note = FALSE). as_structured() reads the default object: one "summary" row per item, token "pct" for each percentage column (with scale_level, the level it shows, missing on the column of missing answers, and top with top_levels on the summary column), "n" and "p". inline() cites a cell: inline(x, item, "Agree", "pct"), with model = "Female" under by.

Items and levels

The items of a battery share one scale. Without levels, the scale is read from the items:

  • items that declare their levels, factors and labelled columns with value labels (as "[code] label", the conversion of freq() and table_categorical()), must declare the same set. An item whose levels differ is an error (class spicy_invalid_input) that names it with its levels. The same set in another order is accepted, and the columns follow the order of the first item;

  • items that declare none, numeric, character and logical columns, take the union of the values they hold: numbers sorted, text in the order of first appearance across the items, so a level that one item alone holds is a column of every item;

  • a mix of the two kinds is an error that names the first item of the other kind.

Given, levels is the scale, and nothing is refused: a level that no item holds shows at 0, and every other answer, observed or declared, is left out of the percentages and the base and named in the note. An item without any answer shows a dash. Declared missing values of a labelled column (na_values, na_range) are missing.

A level that no respondent chose keeps its column, at 0, as a level of the scale that was offered and not chosen. A dash marks a cell with no base: an item without a valid answer, in the table or in a group.

The percentages are row percentages: those of an item sum to 100 over the levels shown (the column of missing answers included under drop_na = FALSE). Its base, n, is its valid answers on the levels shown, or every row under drop_na = FALSE; an answer that levels leaves out is out of the base either way. A percentage carries no more digits than its denominator, so a base of fewer than 100 respondents takes whole percentages: percent_digits = 0 prints them.

The table computes no mean or score of the scale: the levels of a rating scale are ordered, not spaced on an interval.

Tests

With by, each item gets a test of independence of the item and the group, on its table of the levels shown by the groups, its missing answers left out whatever drop_na. The test is the one test chooses, with the rule of table_categorical(): under "auto", the Pearson chi-squared test, without continuity correction, when every expected count is at least 5, and Fisher's exact test otherwise; when the exact enumeration fails, the p-value is its Monte Carlo estimate over 2000 tables, which draws from the session's RNG. A level or a group that holds no answer to the item leaves its table. An item left with one level has no test: its p cell shows a dash and the note names it. An item with answers in fewer than two groups has no test either, and its p cell is blank. Without by, the table runs no test.

Fisher's exact test and its mid-p version condition on counts. Under weights that are not whole numbers, test = "fisher" and test = "midp" are an error (class spicy_unsupported), and an item that "auto" or "n1" would send to Fisher's exact test keeps the chi-squared test, with a warning (class spicy_fallback).

Multiple-comparison adjustment

The items of a battery are read together, as a family of tests, so the p column is adjusted by Holm's method by default, as for the items of table_multiresponse(). Holm's method controls the family-wise error rate whatever the dependence between the items. The raw p-values stay in the long output as p_unadjusted, and in col_meta$p$p_unadjusted of as_structured(). The note names the method and the number of items adjusted together.

See also

table_categorical() for one block of rows per variable, table_multiresponse() for a "check all that apply" question; the article Item batteries.

Examples

# The four life_sat_* items of sochealth rate satisfaction with four
# domains of life on the same scale, from 1 to 5.
sat <- sochealth[c("sex", "age_group")]
scale_labels <- c(
  "Very dissatisfied", "Dissatisfied", "Neutral",
  "Satisfied", "Very satisfied"
)
for (v in grep("^life_sat_", names(sochealth), value = TRUE)) {
  sat[[v]] <- factor(sochealth[[v]], levels = 1:5, labels = scale_labels)
  attr(sat[[v]], "label") <- attr(sochealth[[v]], "label")
}

# One row per item, one column per level, row percentages and the base.
table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), labels = TRUE)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Very dissatisfied  Dissatisfied 
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │        7.4             14.2     
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │        7.6             16.3     
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │        3.1             10.9     
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │        6.4             17.1     
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Neutral  Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │  24.0      25.1    
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │  26.4      30.3    
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │  26.3      29.7    
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │  26.0      31.5    
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Very satisfied   n   
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │      29.4       1192 
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │      19.5       1192 
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │      29.9       1192 
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │      19.0       1192 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: respondents who answered the item.

# The top of the scale, the items sorted on it.
table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  top = c("Very satisfied", "Satisfied"),
  sort = "top-",
  percent_digits = 0
)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very dissatisfied  Dissatisfied  Neutral  Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_relationships │         3               11         26        30     
#>  life_sat_health        │         7               14         24        25     
#>  life_sat_standard      │         6               17         26        31     
#>  life_sat_work          │         8               16         26        30     
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very satisfied  Very satisfied + Satisfied   n   
#> ────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_relationships │       30                    60              1192 
#>  life_sat_health        │       29                    54              1192 
#>  life_sat_standard      │       19                    51              1192 
#>  life_sat_work          │       19                    50              1192 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: respondents who answered the item.

# By sex: the top of the scale in each group, and a test per item.
table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  by = sex,
  top = c("Very satisfied", "Satisfied")
)
#> Item battery by sex
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Female Very satisfied + Satisfied  Female n 
#> ────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │               52.9                   616    
#>  life_sat_work          │               49.1                   615    
#>  life_sat_relationships │               59.8                   615    
#>  life_sat_standard      │               50.9                   615    
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Male Very satisfied + Satisfied  Male n   p   
#> ────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │              56.1                 576    .798 
#>  life_sat_work          │              50.4                 577    .052 
#>  life_sat_relationships │              59.4                 577    .798 
#>  life_sat_standard      │              50.1                 577    .397 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: respondents who answered the item. Item p-values: Pearson chi-squared test of each item by group. Adjusted for 4 tests (Holm method).

# The neutral level left out of the base, missing answers shown.
table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  levels = scale_labels[-3],
  drop_na = FALSE
)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very dissatisfied  Dissatisfied  Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │        9.6             18.5        32.7    
#>  life_sat_work          │       10.2             21.9        40.8    
#>  life_sat_relationships │        4.2             14.7        40.0    
#>  life_sat_standard      │        8.5             22.9        42.1    
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very satisfied  (Missing)   n  
#> ────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │      38.3          0.9     914 
#>  life_sat_work          │      26.2          0.9     885 
#>  life_sat_relationships │      40.3          0.9     886 
#>  life_sat_standard      │      25.5          0.9     890 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: all respondents but those whose answer is left out, including those who did not answer the item. Answers left out of the percentages and the base: Neutral.

# The integer items as they are: `levels` gives the scale.
table_battery(sochealth, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), levels = 1:5)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable                 │   1      2       3       4       5       n    
#> ──────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health          │  7.4    14.2    24.0    25.1    29.4    1192  
#>  life_sat_work            │  7.6    16.3    26.4    30.3    19.5    1192  
#>  life_sat_relationships   │  3.1    10.9    26.3    29.7    29.9    1192  
#>  life_sat_standard        │  6.4    17.1    26.0    31.5    19.0    1192  
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: respondents who answered the item.

# Long data frame.
head(table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), output = "long"))
#>          variable           label             level .row_role   n       pct
#> 1 life_sat_health life_sat_health Very dissatisfied     level  88  7.382550
#> 2 life_sat_health life_sat_health      Dissatisfied     level 169 14.177852
#> 3 life_sat_health life_sat_health           Neutral     level 286 23.993289
#> 4 life_sat_health life_sat_health         Satisfied     level 299 25.083893
#> 5 life_sat_health life_sat_health    Very satisfied     level 350 29.362416
#> 6   life_sat_work   life_sat_work Very dissatisfied     level  90  7.550336

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("tinytable", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tt <- table_battery(
    sat,
    select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
    by = sex,
    labels = TRUE,
    output = "tinytable"
  )
}
# }
